content:
Construction and erection insurance is assessed against the specific project, its stages and the risks accepted under the contract. It does not guarantee compensation for every problem on a construction site. For a contractor or investor in Moldova, preparation starts with the work description, value, location and actual construction schedule.

This material explains what information to prepare and how to compare proposals. Works, equipment and liability towards other people may have different conditions. The construction contract, applicable permits and legal duties need separate checks with the project's specialists. This article does not replace a site's technical or legal assessment.

Describe the work and its current stage

Specify whether the project is new construction, renovation, an extension or installation of equipment. Explain what has already been done and what remains. A building started by another contractor, or premises operating during renovation, needs a different description from an empty site where work has not begun.

Include special operations: excavation, work at height, equipment erection or intervention near existing installations. Use the project's documents without inventing inspections or approvals. The insurer needs to identify the actual subject of the assessment, not just the general word construction.

Identify participants and agreed responsibilities

Identify the investor, contractor, subcontractors and suppliers. Record who buys materials, who stores them and who installs equipment. Ask which persons and interests are included in the proposal. Participation in the same project does not automatically establish that every company and all its property are insured.

Extract insurance requirements from the construction contract and the client's documentation. Separate commercial requirements from legal obligations. Present requested limits, wording and documents before comparing prices. A policy with a suitable name but a different subject may not meet the project's requirement.

Works, materials and temporary structures

The public MOLDASIG page cited in the Romanian original lists works, materials, equipment and temporary structures as potential subjects for assessment. Prepare a project-specific inventory: what is being built, what arrives on site and which auxiliary installations are used. Confirmation belongs in the individual proposal, not in this list.

Explain whether materials are stored on site, elsewhere or are still in transit. Record their owner and the point of delivery. An invoice or inclusion in a budget does not establish protection throughout every stage. Ask for the boundaries between transport, storage and actual incorporation into the works.

Prepare the project value

Use the contract, budget and supporting records to describe the value of the works. Identify client-supplied property and hired equipment separately. Ask which valuation basis is accepted and which expenses must be declared. An estimate for an initial discussion should not be presented as a confirmed final sum.

If the project expands, explain what changes from the original version. Keep records of changes in quantities, technical solutions and schedule. A value declared at the start does not automatically describe the investment after additional work. Request a review of insurance documents whenever project information changes.

Location and neighbouring property matter

Describe access, terrain and nearby buildings. Record occupied premises, other businesses, existing installations and neighbouring public areas. Use observed circumstances and available documentation. An online article cannot establish the condition of the ground, underground networks or a neighbouring building's structural strength.

For work affecting existing elements, ask for the scope of assessed property and operations to be defined. Identify who checks the technical position before work and how findings are recorded. Indicative photographs are not an expert survey. Insurance does not replace design, supervision or safety measures.

Site machinery is not the same as the works

List machinery with owners, identifiers and places of use. A hired excavator, a subcontractor's machine and an installation awaiting erection serve different purposes. Ask which objects are accepted and at which stages protection can be considered.

Discuss machinery transport, operation, storage and internal breakdown separately. Equipment being necessary for construction does not establish that every failure falls within site insurance. Keep hire and maintenance records. Do not infer product conditions from an equipment name.

Include erection, testing and handover in the schedule

Prepare a schedule showing materials delivery, main works, installation and testing. Include staged acceptance and areas brought into use before completion of the whole project. Ask when protection starts and ends for each situation under discussion.

A construction delay does not automatically extend the period written in a policy. Request a review of changes before expiry. Read any defects-remediation period separately from construction and testing. A warranty term in a building contract does not confirm identical conditions under insurance.

Review third-party liability separately

Identify people and property outside the works that could be affected by operations. Explain how access routes and areas of continuing activity are separated. These questions help describe risk; they do not predetermine a company's liability or acceptance of a claim.

Ask about the liability section, included persons and its limits. Do not automatically extend it to employee accidents, the designer's professional liability or the client's penalties. Each may need a separate review. Keep a table distinguishing confirmed items from those outside the proposal.

Works insurance and a performance guarantee are different

Insurance for physical damage to the works must not be confused with an instrument required to secure contractual obligations. Identify the objective first: repairing damage or meeting the client's guarantee requirement. Comparing different documents solely on price can lead to an unsuitable choice.

For a guarantee, check the required form, accepted issuer and wording. For site insurance, check property, events, period and exclusions. Do not state that either document replaces the other without the client's confirmation and a review of the terms. The distinction matters even if both requirements appear in one contract.

Compare requested risks, not product labels

Request a clear list of accepted events and exclusions, meaning situations without cover. For special operations, seek written answers to project-specific questions. Commercial names and general all-risks wording do not mean protection without limits, documents or conditions.

The excess or deductible is the part of a loss borne by the insured under the contract. Compare its operation and limits on separate expenses, including intervention or clean-up if proposed. The insurance premium is the amount paid for insurance. Price comparison is useful only on the same project description and conditions.

When premises remain open during the work

For a shop or office continuing to operate during renovation, describe how the construction area is separated from normal activities. Record customer and employee routes, where existing property is stored and who coordinates interventions. Identify periods when systems are shut down or access changes. These details should not disappear under the general description interior work.

Ask for confirmation of the existing objects and activities considered in the proposal. Damage to new works and damage to furniture already in use are separate questions. Safe organization remains the responsibility of competent project participants. A policy does not replace it.

Preparation checklist for a Moldovan construction project

  • Construction contract and the client's insurance requirements.
  • Technical description and current stage.
  • Budget, values and property supplied by other parties.
  • Schedule, tests and staged handovers.
  • Location, neighbours and existing elements.
  • Contractors, subcontractors and their roles.
  • Machinery inventory and hired equipment.
  • Known problems, incidents and project changes.

Send necessary information through the agreed channel. Do not publish sensitive plans or personal details from project files in an open form. This list is an organizational recommendation, not a universal legal requirement. Documents needed for assessment are confirmed for the specific project and product.

After an incident and before an extension

Apply safety measures and the notification procedure in the existing contract. Preserve facts, findings and intervention records. Do not restart an unsafe installation to demonstrate operation or alter evidence of damage. Technical assessment and insurance assessment serve different roles and need accurate documentation.

Before an extension, update the stage, values and remaining period. Explain which parts have been accepted and which work continues. The broker can help organize comparisons. Risk acceptance and claims handling belong to the insurer under the applicable documents. Acceptance of every project is not promised.

Frequently asked questions

Does site insurance automatically include hired machinery?

Do not assume inclusion. Present the inventory, owners and operations, then ask which objects and periods are accepted.

Does a delay extend the policy?

Not automatically. Compare the revised schedule with document validity and request a review before expiry.

Does a performance guarantee replace works insurance?

Do not treat them as equivalent. A guarantee requirement and protection against physical damage have distinct subjects and conditions.

Can I use another site's insurance price?

A past price is only a discussion reference. Assessment of the current project depends on its works, values, period and accepted conditions.
